issue_context.title: drivers: fpga: include driver for Lattice iCE40 parts
issue_context.body:
**Is your enhancement proposal related to a problem? Please describe.**
Add support for the iCE40 series of FPGAs from Lattice Semi.

The Lattice iCE40 series of FPGAs are an attractive option for low pin-count and low(er) power applications.

The iCE40 series was the first to receive support from the Open-Source synthesis toolchain ([yosys](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys) / [nextpnr](https://github.com/YosysHQ/nextpnr)). Subsequently, Lattice ECP5, EOS S3, and some Xilinx FPGAs (among others) also received support.

Although using the commercial toolchain is always an option, the fact that several FPGAs have Open-Source synthesis toolchain support is appealing for Zephyr and the community.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
A driver and Devicetree binding to support all or some of the iCE40 series of FPGAs from Lattice in SPI Peripheral configuration mode.

The Lattice Technical Note [FPGA-TN-02001-3.3](https://www.latticesemi.com/view_document?document_id=46502) describes the required I/O resources and general timing requirements. Specifically, Chapter 13 "SPI Slave Configuration".

I/O Resources are outlined in the table below. Some I/O resources may be used for for other purposes after FPGA configuration, as indicated in the "User?" column.

| I/O Resource (Pin) | Required? | User? | Description |
| ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| `SPI_POCI` | Yes | Yes | Peripheral-out, Controller-in data line (aka `MISO`, `SPI_SO`) |
| `SPI_PICO` | Yes | Yes | Peripheral-in, Controller-out data line (aka `MOSI`, `SPI_SI`) |
| `SPI_CLK` | Yes | Yes | SPI clock (aka `SPI_SCK`) |
| `SPI_CS` | Yes | No | SPI Chip-select (aka `SPI_SS`) |
| `CDONE` | Yes | Yes | Configuration Done output from iCE40 |
| `CRESET_B` | Yes | No | Configuration Reset input on iCE40 |

Note: while it may be possible to reduce the pin count via careful design consideration, for the purposes of Zephyr integration and in the interest of maximizing system determinism, all I/O resources will be required in DT bindings.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Not having FPGA support.

**Additional context**
This driver will be used on the ICE-V Wireless board (#48217)

review_comments: Could you explain why this is needed? It seems you are setting `n` to `0` anyway? If you just need a constant delay, is there any reason why we can't just use `k_sleep` or `k_busy_wait` instead of this?

This is a calibrated delay loop for nanosecond-scale delays. It should be finely tunable and is controlled by a devicetree parameter. E.g. on esp32-c3, if the delay is zero, then I'm able to generate a 2.2 MHz square wave. If it's set to something non-zero (I can't remember exactly atm), then it can be tuned to generate a 1 MHz square wave. The esp32-c3 has an 80 MHz clock. On faster systems, this becomes more critical to ensure that bit-banging is actually slowed-down enough. 

k_sleep invokes the scheduler, so that's out of the question, and k_busy_wait works in units of microseconds using ticks, so it's also out of the question.

I did use k_busy_wait below to "wait at least several hundred nanoseconds" which gets rounded up to microsecond granularity, but that's far too coarse here.
ack, could you please elaborate this a little bit more in the dts docs or add some comments? Currently the usage description is not very clear
It was already described in the DTS bindings, but I've added some additional comments in the source.
